an2.43:1.3: Here the Sanskrit equivalent of Pali _vagga_ is _vyagra_ (“disunited”), not _varga_ (“group, chapter”).
an2.47:1.3: “Highfalutin talk” is _okkācita_, cf. Sanskrit root _kac_ in the sense “sound, cry”, with prefix _ud-_, “up”.
an2.47:1.5: Such discourses by the Buddha himself, which are also referred to at [an2.47:1.5](), [an5.79:5.2](), and [sn55.53:2.2](), contrast with the frivolous poetry of outsiders or disciples. Unsurprisingly, the Vedas take the opposite stance, for there it is the poets whose insight is “deep” (Rig Veda 2.21.4, 8.8.2; Atharva Veda 4.26.3). | “Deep” (_gambhīra_) emphasizes substantial understanding rather than surface appearance ([an4.104]()). | “Deep in meaning” (_gambhīrattha_) implies both richness in textual implications, as well as profundity of purpose. | “Transcendent” (_lokuttara_) emphasizes that the teachings lead beyond the mundane concerns of worldly life. | The phrase “dealing with emptiness” (_suññatappaṭisaṁyutta_) locates the Buddha’s teachings in relation to his rejection of the Vedic _ātman_ ([mn43:33.1]()), while also pointing to the practice of seclusion and solitude in developing meditation ([mn121]()). Ultimately it refers to Nibbāna as the emptiness of greed, hate, and delusion ([mn43:37.4]()).
an2.50:1.3: The Pali abbreviates, but the explanation should be as the previous Sutta.
